Trainer liability vs owner liability

Trainer liability and owner liability are different questions about a person’s role in an incident involving a horse. Ownership alone does not describe who selected the rider, supplied tack, supervised the activity or knew about a hazard. Compare each person’s conduct with the documents and the governing state law before assuming one role carries every risk.

Publisher: Wise Covington PLLC · Updated 2026-11-03

How do the trainer’s and owner’s roles differ?

Start with the activity and the participant, not just the horse’s owner. Record who arranged the session, selected or approved the rider, provided instructions and controlled the setting. A person can occupy more than one role, so a job label is not a substitute for the sequence of events.

Which facts need to be compared?

Question to resolveRecord to check
Rider selectionTrainer: instructions and assessment; owner: information supplied and any participation in the choice.
Horse and equipmentIdentify who supplied each and what was known about condition or limitations.
SupervisionIdentify who directed the session and controlled the activity when the incident occurred.
Documents and insuranceRead each party’s agreements and policy terms rather than assuming one policy protects everyone.

Preserve the training agreement, releases, tack records, instructions and relevant communications. Identify who supplied the horse and equipment and what was known about the rider and any relevant limitations. Keep observed facts separate from conclusions about blame.

State equine-activity laws differ. North Carolina, for example, addresses inherent risks and also names circumstances that can preserve liability, including certain equipment and participant-ability issues. It is not a blanket assurance that either an owner or a trainer is immune. The statute’s application needs the actual facts.

Does signing a waiver settle responsibility?

A waiver, an equine-activity statute and an insurance policy serve different purposes. Review the wording, parties, activity and applicable state rules together. None should be described as a promise that every claim is barred or every loss is covered.

Where can the underlying rules be checked?

North Carolina equine-activity liability statute (a state-specific example). A state example does not establish the rule in another jurisdiction. Educational only; not legal advice. No endorsements or rankings.
